questions.stem: Atherosclerosis involves the build-up of fatty deposits (plaques) in artery walls. How does this lead to a heart attack?

options.text: The plaque poisons the heart muscle directly
The plaque narrows the coronary artery, reducing blood flow; if a blood clot forms on the plaque, it can completely block the artery, starving heart muscle of oxygen
The plaque causes the heart to beat too fast
The plaque dissolves the artery wall

questions.explanation: Atherosclerotic plaques narrow the coronary arteries, reducing blood flow to the heart muscle. The rough plaque surface can trigger blood clot formation (thrombosis). If a clot blocks the artery completely, the heart muscle beyond the blockage is deprived of oxygen and glucose, causing cell death -- this is a myocardial infarction (heart attack).

questions.stem: A patient with severe coronary artery disease is offered a stent. What does a stent do?

options.text: It replaces the blocked artery with an artificial tube
It is a small mesh tube inserted into the narrowed artery to hold it open, restoring blood flow
It dissolves the fatty deposits in the artery
It bypasses the heart entirely

questions.explanation: A coronary stent is a small wire mesh tube that is inserted into the narrowed artery using a catheter (usually through the groin or wrist). When expanded, it pushes the artery walls apart, holding the artery open to maintain blood flow. Some stents are coated with drugs to prevent re-narrowing. It is a less invasive alternative to bypass surgery.

questions.stem: Statins are prescribed to many patients at risk of cardiovascular disease. How do statins help reduce this risk?

options.text: They thin the blood to prevent clotting
They lower blood cholesterol levels by inhibiting cholesterol production in the liver, slowing plaque formation
They strengthen the heart muscle
They widen the blood vessels permanently

questions.explanation: Statins reduce the level of LDL ('bad') cholesterol in the blood by inhibiting the enzyme HMG-CoA reductase in the liver. Lower cholesterol means less fatty material available to form atherosclerotic plaques. However, statins must be taken long-term, may have side effects, and work best alongside lifestyle changes.

questions.stem: A patient has a faulty heart valve that does not close properly, allowing blood to leak backwards. What treatment option is available?

options.text: Statins to strengthen the valve
Surgical replacement with a mechanical valve or a biological valve (from a pig or cow)
A stent inserted into the valve
Antibiotics to repair the valve tissue

questions.explanation: Faulty heart valves can be replaced surgically. Options include mechanical valves (durable but require lifelong blood-thinning medication to prevent clots) or biological valves (from pigs/cows, which do not require blood thinners but may need replacing after 10-15 years). The choice depends on the patient's age and circumstances.

questions.stem: Which lifestyle factors increase the risk of cardiovascular disease?

options.text: Regular exercise, balanced diet, and not smoking
Smoking, high-fat diet, lack of exercise, and excessive alcohol consumption
Eating too many fruits and vegetables
Drinking too much water and sleeping too long

questions.explanation: Major risk factors for CVD include smoking (damages artery walls), high-fat/high-salt diet (increases cholesterol and blood pressure), lack of exercise (reduces cardiovascular fitness), obesity, excessive alcohol, and stress. Many of these are modifiable lifestyle factors, meaning changes in behaviour can significantly reduce CVD risk.
